In [[statistical physics]], '''mode-coupling theory''' ('''MCT''') is a
family of approximations for the dynamics of many-body systems.
In MCT, a relaxation rate or transport coefficient is
expressed through the nonlinear coupling of a few slow collective
variables ("modes"), and the resulting equations are closed
[[Self-consistency|self-consistently]].
The name covers two bodies of work that are historically connected
but differ in scope and technique:

* the mode-coupling theory of [[Critical phenomena|critical dynamics]], developed in the 1960s mainly by [[Kyozi Kawasaki]], which explains the anomalous transport coefficients near [[critical point (thermodynamics)|critical points]] and was later extended to long-time tails and to the kinetic theory of dense liquids;
* the mode-coupling theory of liquids and [[colloid]]al suspensions, developed from 1984 by [[Wolfgang Götze]] and co-workers.

==Common framework==

Both variants start from the exact equations of motion for
time [[correlation function (statistical mechanics)|correlation functions]]
that follow from the [[Mori–Zwanzig formalism|projection operator formalism]]
of [[Robert Zwanzig]] and Hazime Mori.<ref name="Zwa61"/><ref name="Mor65"/>
For a normalized correlation function <math>\phi(t)</math> of a
conserved or otherwise slow variable, this formalism yields a
generalized [[Langevin equation]] of the form

:<math>\partial_t\phi(t) + \Gamma\phi(t)
  + \int_0^t\!\mathrm{d}t'\,M(t-t')\,\phi(t') = 0,</math>

where the ''memory kernel'' <math>M(t)</math> is itself a correlation
function of the fluctuating forces, which evolve under a projected
dynamics. Equivalently, a transport coefficient <math>L</math> is
given by a [[Green–Kubo relations|Green–Kubo formula]] as the
time integral of a flux autocorrelation function.
These relations are exact but not closed.
The mode-coupling approximation closes them in two steps:

# the fluctuating force (or flux) is projected onto ''products'' of slow variables, typically pairs <math>A_{\mathbf k}B_{\mathbf q-\mathbf k}</math> of Fourier components;
# the resulting four-point correlation functions are factorized into products of two-point functions, <math>\langle A_{\mathbf k}(t)B_{\mathbf p}(t)\, A^*_{\mathbf k}B^*_{\mathbf p}\rangle \approx \langle A_{\mathbf k}(t)A^*_{\mathbf k}\rangle \langle B_{\mathbf p}(t)B^*_{\mathbf p}\rangle.</math>

The memory kernel thereby becomes a quadratic functional of the very
correlation functions it determines.
The so obtained equation of motion of the correlation functions
is genuinely non-linear,
which is decisive for the explanation slow dynamics.
